title: Toothbrushing & interdental cleaning
blurb: Effective brushing technique, manual vs powered brushes, choosing interdental aids, and using disclosing agents to show patients their plaque.
question: A patient with red, puffy gums says he scrubs hard from side to side for about 20 seconds twice a day, and stopped flossing because 'it made my gums bleed'. What would you tell him about his technique, his brushing time and the bleeding?

teach.body: Toothbrushing does two jobs: it removes plaque, which causes gingivitis, periodontal disease and caries, and it delivers fluoride to the teeth. Plaque gathers most at the gum margin and between the teeth, which are exactly the areas a quick or careless brush misses. DBOH advises brushing the gum line and each tooth at least twice a day, last thing at night and on one other occasion, using a method shown by the dental team.

items.label: a day: last thing at night + one other time
each time; 20 seconds is far too short
bristles angled towards the gum margin
replace brush or head, sooner if splayed

items: Put the right amount of fluoride toothpaste on a small-headed, medium-texture brush.
Angle the bristles at about 45° to where the tooth meets the gum.
Use small, gentle, vibrating or circular movements, a couple of teeth at a time.
Work in a set order so every surface is reached: outer, inner and biting surfaces, upper and lower.
Keep going for about 2 minutes. Light pressure only: don't scrub.
Spit out the excess toothpaste; don't rinse.

rows.label: Technique
values: Guide tooth by tooth, no scrubbing

teach.caption: The best brush is the one the patient will use well. Splayed bristles clean poorly, so replace sooner if needed.

teach.body: A toothbrush can't reach the spaces between teeth, where gum disease often starts. DBOH advises adults to clean between the teeth daily, to just below the gum line, before brushing. It is prevention, so it should be done everywhere every day, not only where food gets stuck. Where there's room, an interdental brush is the first choice, sized to fit snugly without forcing. For tight contacts use floss or tape. A single-tufted brush reaches awkward areas.

children.label: Interdental brush
children.sub: Largest size that fits without force

children.label: Floss or tape
children.sub: Floss holder if hard to use

teach.caption: If floss keeps shredding or the patient can't manage it, review technique and offer an alternative aid rather than letting them give up.

teach.body: Plaque is hard to see because it's almost the same colour as teeth. Disclosing tablets or solution contain a dye (often erythrosine) that stains plaque so the patient can see exactly what they're missing. Two-tone agents stain newer plaque pink and older, more established plaque blue or purple. Use them during oral hygiene instruction, when recording plaque scores, and to check progress. Warn patients about temporary staining and protect lips with petroleum jelly.

teach.caption: Plaque and calculus built up at the gum margins, with red, swollen gums that bleed easily. This is why brushing must focus on the gum line and between the teeth.

teach.body: Hard, side-to-side scrubbing, especially with a hard brush, causes toothbrush abrasion and gum recession: switch to a gentle, controlled technique with light pressure. After acidic food or drink, wait about an hour before brushing, as enamel is softened. For patients with gum disease, focus on the gum margin and between the teeth. With extensive inflammation, DBOH suggests getting brushing right first, then adding interdental cleaning. Patients with implants need the same care.

teach.text: Bleeding when brushing or flossing is a sign of inflammation, not a reason to stop. Advise the patient to keep cleaning gently every day; as the plaque is removed and the gums heal, the bleeding usually settles.

items: Brush twice a day for 2 minutes, bristles at 45° to the gum margin, gentle systematic strokes.
Manual or powered are both fine; small head, medium texture; replace every 3 months or when splayed.
Clean between teeth daily before brushing: interdental brush where it fits, floss or tape for tight spaces.
Disclosing agents show plaque; two-tone shows new (pink) and older (blue/purple) plaque.
Bleeding gums mean keep cleaning gently; hard scrubbing causes abrasion and recession.

summary: You can now teach a systematic brushing technique, give the key numbers (twice daily, 2 minutes, 45°, replace every 3 months), compare manual and powered brushes, choose the right interdental aid, use disclosing agents in oral hygiene instruction, and answer common worries such as bleeding gums and hard scrubbing.

A.q: A patient brushes for 20 seconds twice a day with a good technique. How should you interpret this?
options: Brushing time is too short to clean well
Twenty seconds is ideal if the paste foams
Time is irrelevant if technique is good
Short brushing is fine after meals
A.why: About 2 minutes is needed to clean all surfaces systematically; 20 seconds will miss areas.

whyNot.1: Foaming has nothing to do with how well plaque is removed.
whyNot.2: Both technique and time matter; good strokes need time to reach every surface.
whyNot.3: Brushing after meals doesn't make a very short brush effective.

A.q: A patient says their gums bleed when they floss, so they've stopped. What is the best advice?
options: Use mouthwash instead for a month
A.why: Bleeding signals inflammation caused by plaque; gentle daily cleaning removes the plaque and lets the gums heal.

whyNot.0: Stopping leaves plaque in place, so the inflammation continues.
whyNot.1: Mouthwash can't remove plaque from between the teeth.
whyNot.2: Weekly cleaning isn't enough to control plaque and inflammation.

A.q: Which aid is primarily designed to clean between teeth where there is space for it?
A.why: An interdental brush, sized to fit snugly, is the first choice for cleaning between teeth where there's room.

whyNot.0: A tongue scraper cleans the tongue, not between the teeth.
whyNot.2: A single-tufted brush is for awkward areas such as around brackets, not the main interdental aid.
whyNot.3: A disclosing tablet shows plaque; it doesn't remove it.

B.q: A patient scrubs hard from side to side because it 'feels cleaner'. What is the best advice?
options: Carry on if it doesn't hurt
Use a gentle technique, light pressure
Press harder on the visibly stained areas
B.why: Gentle, controlled strokes with light pressure clean effectively without causing abrasion and recession.

whyNot.0: A hard brush makes abrasion and recession more likely.
whyNot.1: Damage from scrubbing builds up painlessly over time.

B.q: A patient only cleans between the teeth where food gets stuck. What does this suggest?
options: Only back teeth need interdental cleaning
Food packing shows there's no plaque
B.why: Interdental cleaning is a daily preventive habit for all spaces, not just a response to trapped food.

whyNot.0: Plaque builds up between all teeth, so the routine misses most areas.
whyNot.2: All interdental spaces collect plaque, front and back.
whyNot.3: Food packing doesn't mean plaque is absent; plaque is present regardless.

B.q: During oral hygiene instruction, which sequence describes effective brushing?
options: Rinse, add paste, brush the front teeth, rinse
Paste on, scrub hard, rinse well, finish
Brush the tongue, add paste, rinse, stop
Paste, bristles at gum line, set order, spit
B.why: Effective brushing means toothpaste on, bristles angled at the gum margin, a systematic order, then spit without rinsing.

whyNot.0: Rinsing removes fluoride, and brushing only the front misses most surfaces.
whyNot.1: Hard scrubbing causes abrasion, and rinsing washes away fluoride.
whyNot.2: This skips the teeth and gum margin, which are where plaque does harm.

C.q: A patient's toothbrush is two years old and the bristles are splayed. What should you advise?
options: Replace it, as it will clean poorly
Keep it, as old brushes are gentler
Keep it if fluoride paste is used
C.why: Splayed bristles remove plaque poorly; brushes or heads should be replaced about every 3 months, or sooner if splayed.

whyNot.1: Worn bristles are less effective, not better.
whyNot.2: Fluoride paste doesn't make up for a worn brush.

C.q: What does a two-tone disclosing agent show when it stains plaque blue or purple?
options: Fresh plaque formed in the last day
C.why: Two-tone agents stain newer plaque pink and older, more established plaque blue or purple.

whyNot.0: New plaque stains pink with a two-tone agent.
whyNot.1: Disclosing agents stain plaque, not subgingival calculus.

C.q: A patient has very tight contacts between their back teeth. Which interdental aid is most suitable?
C.why: Where spaces are too tight for an interdental brush, DBOH advises floss or tape.

whyNot.0: A large brush won't fit a tight contact and could damage the gum.
whyNot.2: A tongue scraper doesn't clean between teeth.
whyNot.3: Toothpicks can damage the gum and don't clean tight contacts well.

reteach.title: Cleaning a fence, not a wall
reteach.question: Imagine your teeth are a row of fence panels with gaps between them. A broom cleans the front of each panel. What happens to the gaps?

blocks.h: The brush cleans the panels, not the gaps
blocks.body: A toothbrush is like a broom: brilliant on the flat fronts and backs, but it can't get into the narrow gaps between the panels. Dirt left in the gaps is where the gum trouble starts. So you need a second tool, an interdental brush or floss, to clean each gap once a day. And you sweep the bottom edge of each panel carefully, because that's where the panel meets the ground: the gum line.

blocks.h: A daily routine that covers everything

steps.label: Between the teeth
steps.sub: Interdental brush or floss, once a day

blocks.text: Pressure doesn't equal clean. Gentle and thorough beats hard and fast, which wears teeth and gums away.

explain.body: Bristles at about 45° to the gum margin, small gentle movements, a set order so no surface is missed, about 2 minutes, then spit, don't rinse.

explain.caption: Plaque left at the gum margin causes gingivitis. Aim the bristles here.

test.q: Where should the toothbrush bristles be aimed to remove the plaque that causes gingivitis?
options: The tips of the front teeth
test.why: Plaque at the gum margin causes gingivitis, so bristles are angled at about 45° towards it.

whyNot.0: Biting surfaces matter for caries, but gingivitis starts at the gum margin.
whyNot.2: Tongue cleaning helps breath, but it doesn't remove plaque from the gum margin.
whyNot.3: Incisal tips aren't where gum-disease plaque collects.

explain.body: Manual or powered brushes are both effective. Choose a small head and medium texture. Replace the brush or head about every 3 months, or sooner if the bristles splay.

test.q: Which toothbrush does DBOH suggest for most patients?
test.why: DBOH suggests a small toothbrush head with medium texture, manual or powered.

whyNot.0: Hard bristles risk abrasion and a large head reaches back teeth poorly.
whyNot.1: A large head struggles to reach the back of the mouth.
whyNot.2: Extra-hard bristles risk abrasion and recession.

explain.body: Clean between the teeth daily, before brushing. Use an interdental brush where it fits, floss or tape for tight spaces, and a single-tufted brush for awkward areas.

test.q: When does DBOH advise adults to clean between their teeth?
options: Only after the scale and polish
test.why: DBOH advises cleaning between the teeth daily, to below the gum line, before toothbrushing.

whyNot.1: Weekly cleaning isn't enough to control plaque.
whyNot.2: Interdental cleaning is preventive, not just reactive.
whyNot.3: It's a daily home habit, not linked to professional cleaning.

explain.body: Disclosing agents stain plaque so patients can see what they miss. Two-tone agents show new plaque pink and older plaque blue or purple. Use them to teach, score plaque and track progress.

explain.caption: Colours vary by product; always follow the manufacturer's guide.

test.q: What is the main purpose of using a disclosing tablet during oral hygiene instruction?
test.why: Disclosing agents stain plaque so the patient can see the areas they are missing when they brush.

whyNot.0: The dye only stains plaque; brushing removes it.
whyNot.1: Disclosing agents temporarily colour plaque, they don't whiten teeth.
whyNot.3: They contain no fluoride for strengthening enamel.
